name: Dart
title: Dart (3.12)
lifecycleNote: superseded by Dart 3.13, shipped with Flutter 3.47.0 on 12 August 2026

type.text: **Sound null safety**: `String` and `String?` are distinct types, and Dart 2.12 and later check the difference at compile time
**Static typing with inference**: `var`, `final`, and `const` infer a type, and that type is checked everywhere the value is used
**Sealed classes give exhaustive matching**: A `sealed class` hierarchy lets the analyser check a `switch` expression for exhaustiveness
**Records give structural data**: `(int, String)` is a value type with no class declaration, and its fields are named or positional
**Pattern matching decouples destructuring from accessors**: An object, list, or record pattern pulls values apart without getter calls
**Extension methods add behaviour outside the type**: An `extension` on `String` adds methods without subclassing or changing the class

construction.text: **`late` decouples initialisation from construction**: A `late final` field is initialised on first access, so the constructor need not compute it
**Factory constructors decouple construction from allocation**: A `factory` constructor can return a cached instance, a subtype, or a constant instead of a fresh object
**`const` constructors build compile-time constants**: A `const` value is canonicalised, so equal constants share one instance
**State lives in the object**: The language forces no global mutable state, and an instance is the natural unit of state
**Named and optional parameters state the construction contract**: `Point({required int x, int y = 0})` names each argument at the call site
**A library-level `var` is global mutable state**: Mutable top-level variables are permitted, so global coupling needs discipline rather than the compiler

memory.text: **The VM collects garbage**: Allocation and reclamation are automatic, and the program cannot choose when a pause happens
**No RAII**: The language has no scope-exit destructor, so an opened `File` or socket must be closed by hand or in a `try`/`finally`
**No ownership or borrow model**: Aliasing is unrestricted, so two references can hold the same mutable object and the VM alone tracks its lifetime
**No manual deallocation**: Ordinary Dart never frees memory, so a double free or a use after free cannot occur in managed code
**Each isolate owns a separate heap**: An isolate collects its own garbage, so a pause is confined to one isolate
**`Finalizer` and weak references are best effort**: Finalisation runs when the collector decides, not at a moment the program chooses

error.text: **Exceptions are unchecked**: `throw` accepts any object and no signature declares what a function can throw, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type
**`try`/`on`/`catch`/`finally` gives a structured path**: The recovery path is separate from the normal path, but the caught type is matched at run time
**`Error` and `Exception` are a convention**: `Error` marks a programming fault and `Exception` a recoverable condition, and nothing enforces the split
**`finally` separates cleanup from recovery**: The block runs whether the body succeeds, throws, or returns
**`Future` failures stay inside the chain**: `async`/`await` routes a thrown object to the awaiting caller, and `catchError` handles it beside the value
**`assert` states a precondition in development mode**: An assertion runs in development and JIT mode, so a violated invariant fails early

concurrency.text: **Isolates share no memory**: Each isolate has its own heap and communicates only by message, so a data race between isolates cannot occur
**`Future` and `async`/`await` suspend without blocking**: An `await` yields the event loop instead of holding a thread
**`Stream` composes asynchronous sequences**: `await for` and stream transformers chain events without callback nesting
**No race detection inside an isolate**: The event loop runs each callback to completion, and the language provides no lock or race checker for shared mutable state
**`Isolate.run` and ports marshal by copy**: A message is copied or transferred, so a value cannot be shared accidentally
**One event loop per isolate removes most synchronisation**: Application code on a single isolate needs no lock

platform.text: **Ahead-of-time compilation to native code**: `dart compile exe` and the Flutter release build produce native ARM and x64 binaries with no interpreter
**Web targets are first class**: `dart compile js` and `dart2wasm` emit JavaScript and WebAssembly for browsers
**The development VM supports hot reload**: The kernel VM and the JIT path give an edit-and-reload cycle without a rebuild
**No vendor runtime lock-in**: One source runs on the Dart VM, as native code, and in a browser
**Flutter is the dominant consumer**: Server use through Shelf and Dart Frog is real but far smaller

performance.text: **Production code is compiled ahead of time**: The Flutter release toolchain and `dart compile` emit native machine code, so the hot path holds no interpreter
**Startup is fast**: An AOT binary starts without a warm-up phase, which matters for a mobile cold start
**The JIT optimises development runs**: The development VM profiles and recompiles hot functions, so hot reload keeps speed
**The collector pauses the mutator**: The generational garbage collector stops execution during a collection, which appears as a frame-time spike
**Throughput is good but not hand-tuned C**: AOT output is close to a native compiler's, but a numeric kernel has no SIMD or arena control in the language

ecosystem.text: **`dart pub` and pub.dev are mature**: Version constraints, a lockfile, and a central registry are part of the SDK
**The SDK ships the toolchain**: `dart analyze`, `dart format`, `dart test`, and `dart fix` need no extra install
**Google backs the language**: Funding and staff come from one large vendor, which keeps the toolchain coherent
**The package ecosystem is small outside Flutter**: The great majority of packages are Flutter plugins, so a server or CLI project finds fewer libraries
**Null-safety migration is still in progress for old packages**: An unmigrated dependency weakens the soundness guarantee at the boundary
**A single vendor holds the roadmap**: The language specification and the Flutter release train come from one company
Native code reaches Dart through the FFI's C interface, whose ABI the platform publishes [@dartFfi]

evolution.text: **Dart 3 unified the language at 100% null safety**: One soundness model now applies to all migrated code
**Language versions are declared per library**: A `// @dart=3.0` comment pins a library to a language version, so a migration can be staged
**`dart fix --apply` automates migrations**: Mechanical rewrites for deprecations ship with the SDK
**The language changes on a predictable cadence**: Releases follow the Flutter stable train, so a team can plan an upgrade
**Older packages may lag the current release**: A dependency that targets an older language version keeps its old semantics

domain.text: **Excellent fit for cross-platform UI**: Flutter renders one widget tree on iOS, Android, web, and desktop from one source
**Server-side use is supported**: Shelf and Dart Frog provide HTTP servers and routing on the same runtime
**Browser output works through JavaScript and WebAssembly**: `dart compile js` and `dart2wasm` cover the web target
**Command-line tools are a supported target**: `dart compile exe` produces a standalone binary
**Non-Flutter use is uncommon**: Examples, packages, and hiring lean toward UI development

learning.text: **The syntax is familiar**: The C-style grammar and the type annotations resemble Java, C#, and TypeScript
**Inference keeps annotations light**: `var`, `final`, and collection literals let a beginner write working code early
**The official documentation is thorough**: dart.dev carries a language tour, codelabs, and the effective-Dart guides
**Null safety gives a clear first rule**: The compiler's null-safety errors teach the distinction between `T` and `T?` quickly
**Dart 3 features are recent**: Records, patterns, and sealed classes postdate many tutorials, so older material omits them

syntax.text: **Familiar C-style syntax**: Braces, semicolons, and the `.` member operator match the mainstream
**Expression-oriented `switch`**: A Dart 3 `switch` expression returns a value and reads as a mapping from case to result
**String interpolation is built in**: `"value: $x"` embeds an expression without a concatenation call
**Named arguments make call sites self-documenting**: `theme: dark, dense: true` states the intent at the call
**Asynchronous code colours functions**: An `async` function returns `Future<T>`, so a caller must be asynchronous to await it
**Null-aware operators add punctuation**: `?.`, `!`, and `??` are concise but stack up in dense expressions

testing.text: **`package:test` is the standard runner**: `dart test` discovers files under `test/` and reports structured failures
**`flutter_test` covers widget tests**: `WidgetTester` pumps frames and finds widgets by key or text
**The analyser catches errors before the test run**: `dart analyze` reports type and null-safety faults without executing code
**Asynchronous and golden tests are supported**: `expectLater` and matchers handle `Future` and `Stream` results
**There is no single mocking standard**: `mockito` with code generation and `mocktail` without it are both common

security.text: **Sound null safety removes null dereference**: A `String?` cannot be used as a `String` without a check or an explicit `!`
**Static typing rejects type confusion at compile time**: The analyser rejects an assignment the type system forbids
**Bounds checking is always on**: An index outside a list's range throws `RangeError` rather than reading adjacent memory
**No `eval` and no dynamic code execution**: The language has no construct that turns a string into code
**Web output inherits browser risks**: A compiled script still runs inside the browser's security model

tradeoffs: **The ecosystem outside Flutter is small**: Most packages target Flutter, so a non-UI project has fewer libraries; this is a community outcome, not a language mechanism
**Null-safety migration of old packages is unfinished**: An unmigrated package carries an unsound boundary, and opting out with a `// @dart=2.x` comment is a legacy choice
**JIT in development and AOT in production is a tooling split**: Hot reload needs the JIT, and a release build needs the AOT compiler
**Familiar syntax is a familiarity choice**: The C-style grammar is close to Java and TypeScript, which lowers the barrier but is not a coupling property
**`dart:ffi` reaches native code**: FFI is an explicit escape hatch, so the memory-safety guarantees of managed code do not extend across it
**Dart is a general-purpose language with a UI-heavy reputation**: The reputation follows Flutter, not a scope limit in the language
verdict: Dart's design yields moderate language-imposed coupling. Sound null safety, inference, records, patterns, and sealed classes decouple the type from absence and from shape, and isolates remove shared-memory races entirely. Main strengths: AOT native compilation with fast startup, an explicit `late` and `factory` construction model, and a compiler that rejects null-safety faults before the program runs. Main weaknesses: the collector and the absence of RAII make resource release non-deterministic, exceptions are unchecked, there is no race detection inside an isolate, and the package ecosystem is small outside Flutter.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: A pub package ships source the app build compiles
Native code reaches Dart through the FFI's C interface, whose ABI the platform publishes
